Area.evidence_source: Men in our study spoke about experiencing fragmented pathways to mental health care, and they partly attributed the persistence of their mental health problems to what they viewed as irregular, infrequent, and unpleasant experiences with mental health service providers. Generally, men spoke about a cyclical pattern wherein negative experiences with health care providers were followed by avoidance of health care settings, crisis, and then by involuntary service utilization. Some went from one provider to another (e.g., emergency department, to crisis team, to assessment, to a family doctor) in search of care but were unable to acquire the type of help or referral they sought. This cyclical pattern tended to result in a deterioration of respect for service providers and a sense that they would not receive the help they needed. Specific provider practices, patient practices, and episodes (see Table 2) were noted to contribute to the fragmented pathways. In particular, men identified three personal practices, five health-care provider practices and two types of episodes they believed contributed to their fragmented pathways to care. While the practices and episodes have been separated conceptually, in the sections to follow we attempt to provide a sense of how they interconnect in reality. Table 2. Practices and episodes that contribute to fragment- ed pathways to care Patient practices Failure to identify or acknowledge mental health problems Inability to articulate feelings and emotions Difficulties navigating the referral system Provider practices Distress mislabeled Failure to identify or acknowledge underlying factors Disrespectful treatment of patients Insufficient assessment Overreliance on medications Episodes Use of drastic measures Experience indignities during hospitalization
